John Adams. The second President of the United States, he was a lawyer and political philosopher who shaped the ideological foundations of the American Revolution, drafted the Declaration of Independence, and stewarded the young republic through conflict with France.

As a Massachusetts lawyer, Adams was an early opponent of British authority who rallied opposition to the Stamp Act and became prominent in Massachusetts colonial politics. He served on the Continental Congress where he was instrumental in drafting the Declaration of Independence in 1776, articulating the philosophical case for independence based on natural rights and popular sovereignty.

During and after the Revolutionary War, he served as a diplomat, negotiating the Treaty of Paris in 1783 that ended the war and later serving as minister to France, Britain, and the Dutch Republic. He championed the Constitution at the ratification convention and supported the creation of a strong federal government with separation of powers and checks and balances.

Adams served as the first Vice President under George Washington from 1789 to 1797, a role he found frustrating, before becoming president in 1796 after Washington's retirement. As president, he navigated the Quasi-War, an undeclared conflict with France from 1798 to 1800 over neutral shipping rights, avoiding full war but destabilizing politics.

He signed the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, federal laws restricting free speech and targeting foreign-born and opposition press, laws that became symbols of Federalist overreach and were widely condemned. He lost his re-election bid to Thomas Jefferson in 1800, but his commitment to constitutional processes preserved the transition of power to the opposition party, a contentious transfer that could have shattered the republic.

Adams lived until 1826, long enough to see the republic endure, dying on the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.
